homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: The start of the working week – alarm clocks, the first coffee, “Montag schon wieder!”

examples.text: Am Montag gehe ich wieder zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: On Monday I go back to work.
Today is Monday.
The museum is closed on Mondays.

phrases.meaning: a Monday taken off work without a good reason

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: From Middle High German mōntac, māntac, from Old High German mānotag, from Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag (“day of the moon”), equivalent to Mond + Tag. Compare Dutch maandag, English Monday, Danish mandag.

funFacts: Montag is the “moon day” (Mond + Tag), a calque of Latin dies Lunae; Greek Δευτέρα and Hebrew יוֹם שֵׁנִי count instead: “the second (day)”, and Chinese says 星期一, “week-one”.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Montag – not *in Montag or *an Montag without the article.
Days are masculine: der Montag, plural die Montage.
subtleties: Every Monday = montags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Montags ist das Museum geschlossen.
Ein blauer Montag is a Monday someone skips work (blaumachen = to skive off).

compound.none: one word today; historically “day of Thingsus” (a Germanic god), not Dienst + Tag

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: The second working day – the week has started, the weekend is still far.

examples.text: Am Dienstag habe ich einen Termin beim Arzt.
examples.tr: On Tuesday I have a doctor’s appointment.
Is today Tuesday or Wednesday?
On Tuesdays we always cook soup.

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dingesdach and Middle Dutch dinsendach, replacing older High German forms (Middle High German ziestac, Bavarian Ertag). Probably from Proto-Germanic *þingas-dagaz (“day of Thingsus”, a Germanic god, or “day of the Thing”, the council). Cognate with Dutch dinsdag.

funFacts: English Tuesday is Tiw’s day; German took a different name from the north – southern dialects still say Ertag or Zischtig.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Dienstag – not *in Dienstag or *an Dienstag without the article.
Dienstag is not related to der Dienst (service, duty), although it looks like it.
subtleties: Every Tuesday = dienstags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Dienstags kochen wir immer Suppe.

compound.none: one word today; historically Mitte + Woche (“mid-week”), but masculine like the other days

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Midweek – the hump of the working week.

examples.text: Am Mittwoch fahre ich nach Berlin.
examples.tr: On Wednesday I’m going to Berlin.
It’s Wednesday already today!

examples.text: Mittwochs gehe ich zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: On Wednesdays I walk to work.

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: From Middle High German mittewoche, from Old High German mittawehha (literally “middle of the week”), calqued on Ecclesiastical Latin media hebdomas. Equivalent to Mitte (“middle”) + Woche (“week”); it became masculine after the other weekdays. Compare English midweek.

funFacts: Mittwoch is “mid-week” – the old “Odin’s day” (English Wednesday) was dropped in German long ago; Greek Τετάρτη and Hebrew יוֹם רְבִיעִי count it as “the fourth (day)”.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Mittwoch – not *in Mittwoch or *an Mittwoch without the article.
Mittwoch is the only weekday not ending in -tag, but it is masculine like the others: der Mittwoch (although die Woche is feminine).
subtleties: Every Wednesday = mittwochs (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Mittwochs gehe ich zu Fuß zur Arbeit.

compound.none: one word today; historically “day of Donar” (Thor, the thunder god): Donner + s + Tag

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Almost the weekend – late shopping, evening plans.

examples.tr: My mother is coming on Thursday.
The market is on Thursday.
On Thursdays we eat at the restaurant.

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: From Middle High German donerstac, from Old High German donarestag, from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”). Compare Dutch donderdag, English Thursday, Danish torsdag.

funFacts: Donnerstag is the day of Donar (Thor), the thunder god – der Donner is still “thunder”; it translates Latin dies Iovis (Jupiter’s day), Greek Πέμπτη is simply “the fifth”.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Donnerstag – not *in Donnerstag or *an Donnerstag without the article.
Donnerstag / Dienstag: both start with D – learners mix them up; Donner = thunder helps.
subtleties: Every Thursday = donnerstags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Donnerstags essen wir im Restaurant.

compound.none: one word today; historically “day of Frija” (a Germanic goddess), not frei + Tag

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: The last working day – “Endlich Freitag!”, the weekend is coming.

examples.text: Am Freitag gehen wir ins Kino.
examples.tr: On Friday we’re going to the cinema.
Finally it’s Friday!
On Fridays he always eats fish.

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vrītac, from Old High German frīatag, from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag (“day of Frigg”), calque of Latin dies Veneris. Compare Dutch vrijdag, English Friday, Danish fredag.

funFacts: Freitag translates Latin dies Veneris (Venus’s day) with a Germanic goddess; Arabic الجُمُعَة (Friday) means “the gathering” – the day of the congregational prayer.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Freitag – not *in Freitag or *an Freitag without the article.
Freitag has nothing to do with frei (free) – it is the day of the goddess Frija.
subtleties: Every Friday = freitags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Freitags isst er immer Fisch.
Karfreitag (Good Friday) is a public holiday all over Germany.

compound.none: one word today; from Greek sábbaton (the Sabbath) + Tag

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Shopping, football, the market – the first day of the weekend.

examples.text: Am Samstag kaufen wir auf dem Markt ein.
examples.tr: On Saturday we do our shopping at the market.
I’m off on Saturday.
My son plays football on Saturdays.

synonyms.nuance: Saturday in northern and eastern Germany – literally “Sunday eve”

etymology.text: From Middle High German sameȥtac, from Old High German sambaȥtag (“Sabbath day”), from Gothic *sambatō, an alteration of Biblical sabbatō, from Koine Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”). Compare French samedi, Hungarian szombat.

funFacts: Samstag, Greek Σάββατο, Russian суббота, Arabic السَّبْت (as-sabt) and Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabbat) all come from or share the Semitic word for the Sabbath – one word across the course languages.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Samstag – not *in Samstag or *an Samstag without the article.
North and east say Sonnabend, the rest of Germany, Austria and Switzerland Samstag – both are correct standard German.
subtleties: Every Saturday = samstags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Samstags spielt mein Sohn Fußball.
Many shops close early on Saturday in small towns; on Sunday almost all are closed.

compound.none: one word today; historically Sonne + Tag (“day of the sun”)

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Quiet streets, closed shops, coffee and cake with the family.

examples.text: Am Sonntag besuchen wir meine Oma.
examples.tr: On Sunday we visit my grandma.
On Sundays the shops are closed.

examples.text: Heute ist Sonntag, wir bleiben zu Hause.
examples.tr: Today is Sunday, we’re staying at home.

profile.synonymsNone: A day of the week has no synonym in standard German; regional words are given as variants.

etymology.text: From Middle High German sunne(n)tac, from Old High German sunnūntag, from late Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag (“day of the sun”), a calque of Latin diēs Sōlis. Equivalent to Sonne + Tag. Compare Dutch zondag, English Sunday.

funFacts: Sonntag is the “sun day”; Greek Κυριακή is “the Lord’s day”, and Hebrew יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן (“first day”) and Arabic الأَحَد (“the one”) count it as the first day – the week begins on Sunday there.
pitfalls: On a day = am (an + dem): am Sonntag – not *in Sonntag or *an Sonntag without the article.
In Germany the week starts on Monday; Sunday is the seventh day.
subtleties: Every Sunday = sonntags (lower case, with -s: an adverb): Sonntags sind die Geschäfte zu.
Sonntagsruhe: by law most shops are closed on Sundays and public holidays.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Saturday and Sunday – sleeping in, trips, friends, “Schönes Wochenende!”

examples.text: Am Wochenende fahren wir in die Berge.
examples.tr: At the weekend we’re going to the mountains.
Have a nice weekend!
What are you doing at the weekend?

profile.synonymsNone: No real synonym; WE is only an abbreviation in writing.

etymology.text: Compound of Woche (“week”) + -n- + Ende (“end”). The modern sense since the 19th century after English weekend, in general use since about 1920.

funFacts: Wochenende copies English weekend piece by piece – Greek also uses its own word, Σαββατοκύριακο (“Saturday-Sunday”).
pitfalls: Neuter (because of das Ende): das Wochenende.
At the weekend = am Wochenende (an + dem, like am Montag) – not *im Wochenende.
subtleties: Wochenende is a loan translation of English weekend – one of many words German built from its own parts on an English model.

plurals.note: in the compounds: die Landtage, die Bundestage

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.note: only in compounds: der Landtag, der Bundestag

profile.feeling: The basic unit of life: from morning to night, every day, “Guten Tag!”

senses.def: day (of a meeting): Landtag, Reichstag – an assembly

examples.tr: What day is it today?

examples.text: Ich trinke jeden Tag zwei Tassen Kaffee.
examples.tr: I drink two cups of coffee every day.

examples.text: Wir bleiben drei Tage in Wien.
examples.tr: We’re staying in Vienna for three days.

examples.text: Am Tag ist es warm, in der Nacht kalt.
examples.tr: It’s warm during the day, cold at night.

examples.text: Der Landtag tagt heute in Düsseldorf.
examples.tr: The state parliament is in session in Düsseldorf today.

phrases.text: Morgen ist auch noch ein Tag.
Man soll den Tag nicht vor dem Abend loben.
phrases.tr: Don’t praise the day before the evening.
phrases.meaning: Don’t count your chickens before they hatch.

synonyms.nuance: date – the number of the day in the calendar

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German tac, from Old High German tag, from Proto-West Germanic *dag, from Proto-Germanic *dagaz. From the meaning “a fixed day for a meeting” come Reichstag, Landtag and tagen (“to hold a meeting”).

funFacts: Tag and English day are the same word; Greek ημέρα gives the “ephemeral” (lasting a day).
pitfalls: Masculine: der Tag, plural die Tage, dative plural den Tagen.
Duration needs no preposition: Ich bleibe drei Tage (accusative); für drei Tage is also possible, especially for plans.
jeden Tag (every day) is accusative: jed-en because Tag is masculine.
subtleties: Guten Tag is said from late morning to early evening; Tag! alone is a short casual greeting.
Reichstag and Bundestag are “diets”: assemblies that once met on a fixed day.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Darkness, sleep, stars – and long summer nights out.

examples.text: In der Nacht schläft das Baby gut.
examples.tr: At night the baby sleeps well.
Good night!

examples.text: Wir bleiben zwei Nächte im Hotel.
examples.tr: We’re staying two nights at the hotel.

phrases.tr: to make the night into day

synonyms.nuance: evening – before bedtime; “tonight” for going out is heute Abend

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German naht, from Old High German naht, from Proto-West Germanic *naht, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

funFacts: Nacht, English night, Greek νύχτα (νύξ), Latin nox and Russian ночь all come from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
pitfalls: At night = in der Nacht (in + dative feminine) – the one part of the day that does not take am: am Morgen, am Abend, but in der Nacht.
Plural with umlaut: die Nächte.
subtleties: heute Nacht means tonight or last night – context decides: Heute Nacht habe ich schlecht geschlafen (last night).
nachts (lower case) = at night, every night: Nachts ist es hier ruhig.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Coffee, the first light, “Guten Morgen!” – the hours from waking up to late morning.

senses.def: das Morgen: the future, tomorrow (as a noun)

examples.tr: In the morning I drink coffee.

examples.text: Guten Morgen, wie geht es Ihnen?
examples.tr: Good morning, how are you?

examples.text: Heute Morgen war ich beim Arzt.
examples.tr: This morning I was at the doctor’s.

examples.text: Der Bauer besaß zehn Morgen Land.
examples.tr: The farmer owned ten morgen of land.

examples.text: Niemand weiß, was das Morgen bringt.
examples.tr: Nobody knows what tomorrow brings.

phrases.tr: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
phrases.meaning: The early bird catches the worm.

synonyms.nuance: late morning – from about 9 to 12 o’clock
early morning: in aller Frühe (at the crack of dawn)

etymology.text: From Middle High German morgen, from Old High German morgan, from Proto-West Germanic *morgan, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, from Proto-Indo-European *merkʷ- (“to blink, twinkle”). Compare Dutch morgen, English morn and morrow, Swedish morgon.

funFacts: morgen (tomorrow) grew out of der Morgen: “in the morning” came to mean “the next morning” – English morrow and morning did the same.
pitfalls: der Morgen (morning, capital M) ≠ morgen (tomorrow, lower case); tomorrow morning is morgen früh (not *morgen Morgen).
With heute, gestern the noun keeps its capital: heute Morgen, gestern Morgen.
In the morning = am Morgen; every morning = morgens.
subtleties: Plural die Morgen (same as the singular): Die Morgen sind jetzt kalt.

compound.none: one word today; historically mitt- (“middle”) + Tag

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Midday – the lunch break, the sun at its highest.

examples.text: Am Mittag essen wir in der Kantine.
examples.tr: At midday we eat in the canteen.
At lunchtime today I’m cooking soup.
We’re taking our lunch break now.

etymology.text: From Middle High German mittetac, from Old High German mittitac, compound of mitti (see Mitte) and tac (see Tag). Cognate with Dutch middag.

funFacts: Mittag is “mid-day” (Mitte + Tag), like Dutch middag and Greek μεσημέρι (μέσος + ημέρα, “middle of the day”).
pitfalls: Mittag is a time of day; the meal is das Mittagessen (fd.07): Zu Mittag gibt es Suppe.
zu Mittag essen = to have lunch; am Mittag = at midday.
subtleties: Mittag is not a point but a span, roughly 12 to 2 – noon exactly is zwölf Uhr.
mittags (lower case) = at midday, every midday.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

profile.feeling: Coffee and cake time – Kaffee und Kuchen at four o’clock.

examples.text: Am Nachmittag gehen die Kinder in den Park.
examples.tr: In the afternoon the children go to the park.

examples.text: Heute Nachmittag bin ich zu Hause.
examples.tr: This afternoon I’m at home.
We drink coffee in the afternoon.

synonyms.nuance: after lunch – a looser way to say it

etymology.text: nach (“after”) + Mittag (“midday”). Compare Dutch namiddag.

funFacts: Nachmittag is “after-midday”, the same idea as Latin post meridiem (p.m.) and Greek απόγευμα (after the lunch, γεύμα).
pitfalls: In the afternoon = am Nachmittag; every afternoon = nachmittags.
heute Nachmittag (this afternoon) – Nachmittag keeps its capital.
subtleties: Kaffee und Kuchen at about 3–4 p.m. is a German afternoon institution, especially on Sundays.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: After work: dinner, television, friends – “Guten Abend!”

senses.def: evening event, party: ein bunter Abend

examples.tr: In the evening we eat together.
What are you doing tonight?

examples.text: Guten Abend, meine Damen und Herren!
examples.tr: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen!

examples.text: Der Verein lädt zu einem bunten Abend mit Musik ein.
examples.tr: The club invites everyone to an evening of entertainment with music.

collocations.tr: the end of the working day

phrases.text: Es ist noch nicht aller Tage Abend.
phrases.tr: It is not yet the evening of all days.
phrases.meaning: It’s not over yet; things may still change.

synonyms.nuance: the time after work – literally “celebration evening”: Schönen Feierabend!

etymology.text: From Middle High German ābent, from Old High German āband, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs. Compare Dutch avond, English even (evening) and eve.

funFacts: Abend is English eve and evening – Christmas Eve is Heiligabend, the “holy evening”.
pitfalls: In the evening = am Abend; every evening = abends.
Tonight (going out) = heute Abend, not *heute Nacht.
subtleties: Abend has a long -a- and the stress on A-; plural die Abende.
Heiligabend is Christmas Eve – the main day of Christmas in Germany, when presents are given.

profile.feeling: The day you are living – plans, the date, “today’s” news.

examples.tr: Today is Monday.
What are you cooking today?

examples.text: Heute reisen viele Menschen mit dem Flugzeug.
examples.tr: Nowadays many people travel by plane.

phrases.text: Was du heute kannst besorgen, das verschiebe nicht auf morgen.
phrases.tr: What you can do today, don’t put off till tomorrow.
phrases.meaning: Don’t put off till tomorrow what you can do today.

synonyms.nuance: nowadays – only the “in our time” meaning

etymology.text: From Middle High German hiute, from Old High German hiutu, a contraction of *hiu tagu, from Proto-Germanic *hinō dagō (“on this day”). Compare Old English hēodæġ and Dutch heden.

funFacts: heute is literally “this day” (*hiu tagu) – Greek σήμερα (from ἡμέρα, day) and Turkish bugün (bu gün, “this day”) are built the same way.
pitfalls: heute + a part of the day: heute Morgen, heute Mittag, heute Abend (capital letters), but tonight in bed = heute Nacht.
A time word at the start pushes the verb before the subject: Heute gehe ich … (not *Heute ich gehe …).
subtleties: das Heute (noun) = the present: im Hier und Heute.

profile.feeling: The next day – plans, appointments, “Bis morgen!”

examples.tr: Tomorrow I’m going to Hamburg.
See you tomorrow!
Are you coming tomorrow morning?

synonyms.nuance: the next day – in a story, not counted from today

etymology.text: From Middle High German morgene, from Old High German morgane, from Proto-West Germanic *morgin. Cognate with English morrow, morn.

funFacts: English “morrow” (tomorrow) is the same word; the morning became the next morning in both languages.
pitfalls: morgen (tomorrow, small m) ≠ der Morgen (morning, capital M).
Tomorrow morning = morgen früh – never *morgen Morgen.
German uses the present tense for tomorrow: Morgen fahre ich … (I’m going / I’ll go).
subtleties: übermorgen = the day after tomorrow, vorgestern = the day before yesterday.

profile.feeling: The day just gone – what happened, where you were.

senses.def: in the past (figurative: nicht von gestern)

examples.tr: Yesterday was Sunday.

examples.text: Gestern Abend war ich zu Hause.
examples.tr: Yesterday evening I was at home.

examples.text: Ich bin doch nicht von gestern!
examples.tr: I wasn’t born yesterday!

phrases.meaning: not to be born yesterday, not to be naive

synonyms.nuance: the day before – reports, not counted from today

etymology.text: From Middle High German gestern, from Old High German gesteron, from Proto-West Germanic *gesteran. Cognate with English yester(day) and Dutch gisteren.

funFacts: gestern is the yester- of English yesterday; Greek χθες and Latin heri share the same old root.
pitfalls: gestern needs the past: Gestern war ich zu Hause (war = was, the past of sein – the past comes in the next stage).
Last night (evening) = gestern Abend; last night (in bed) = heute Nacht.
subtleties: gestern Abend, gestern Morgen: the part of the day keeps its capital letter.

profile.feeling: This very moment – “Jetzt oder nie!”

senses.def: now (adding emphasis): Was ist jetzt los?

examples.tr: I’m going home now.
Where are you now?
What do we do now?

synonyms.nuance: now – more written or literary; also “well…” at the start of a sentence

etymology.text: From Middle High German iez, ieze, iezuo, from Old High German iozuo (“straightaway, at once”), equivalent to je + zu. Compare English yet and Yiddish יעצט (yetst).

funFacts: jetzt is related to English yet; Yiddish יעצט (yetst) is the same word written in Hebrew letters.
pitfalls: jetzt (now) and gleich (in a moment) are different: Ich komme gleich = I’m coming in a minute.
subtleties: jetzt is also a filler word that adds urgency: Jetzt sag mal … (Come on, tell me …).

profile.feeling: Not now – a little bit on, after this.

examples.tr: I’ll call you later.
We’ll eat later.
Later he wants to become a doctor.

etymology.text: Comparative of spät (“late”), from Middle High German spǣte, from Old High German spāti.

funFacts: Bis später, bis bald, bis morgen: German says goodbye by naming when you meet again – like Greek τα λέμε αργότερα / αύριο.
pitfalls: später is the comparative of spät (late, later) but works as its own adverb: Ich komme später.
Bis später! = See you later (the same day).
subtleties: nachher is “later today”; später can be minutes or years away.

profile.feeling: Not long now – the holidays, the bus, a visit.

examples.tr: The bus is coming soon.
See you soon!
The holidays are coming soon!

synonyms.nuance: in a moment, right away – sooner than bald

etymology.text: From Middle High German balde, from Old High German baldo, adverb of bald (“bold, quick”), from Proto-Germanic *balþaz. Cognate with Dutch boud, English bold.

funFacts: bald is English bold: being “bold” once meant being quick and keen, so “quickly” became “soon”.
pitfalls: bald (soon) vs. gleich (in a moment): Ich komme gleich (in a minute) – Ich komme bald (soon, some time).
Comparative eher (sooner), not *balder: Ich komme eher.
subtleties: bald … bald … = now … now …: bald hier, bald dort.

contrasts.value: after a day word: morgen früh, heute früh

profile.feeling: The alarm at six, the first train, the market at dawn.

senses.def: in the morning (morgen früh; regionally also heute früh)

examples.tr: I always get up early.

examples.text: Wir fahren morgen früh nach Berlin.
examples.tr: We’re going to Berlin tomorrow morning.

examples.text: Es ist noch zu früh für Wein.
examples.tr: It’s still too early for wine.

examples.text: Ich rufe dich morgen früh an.
examples.tr: I’ll call you tomorrow morning.

phrases.text: Früh übt sich, was ein Meister werden will.
phrases.tr: Early practises who wants to become a master.

synonyms.nuance: early, in good time – southern Germany, Austria

etymology.text: From Middle High German vrüe, vrüeje, from Old High German fruoi, from Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī) (“early”). Cognate with Dutch vroeg.

funFacts: der Frühling (spring) is the “early” part of the year: früh + -ling.
pitfalls: früh is also an adjective: am frühen Morgen (early in the morning) – the ending comes with the noun.
Comparative früher means “earlier” and also “in the past, formerly”: Früher war alles anders.
subtleties: morgen früh is the normal way to say tomorrow morning.

override.pos: Wiktionary files spät only as an adjective; German uses adjectives unchanged as adverbs (Er kommt spät), and the course teaches spät here as the adverb “late” (adv.late).

profile.feeling: The last bus, a long evening – and the question “Wie spät ist es?”

examples.text: Er kommt immer spät nach Hause.
examples.tr: He always comes home late.

examples.text: Es ist schon spät, ich gehe jetzt.
examples.tr: It’s late already, I’m going now.
What time is it?

synonyms.nuance: delayed – trains, planes: Der Zug ist verspätet.

etymology.text: From Middle High German spǣte, from Old High German spāti, from Proto-West Germanic *spādī, from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz. Probably related to sparen (“to spare”).

funFacts: Asking “how late is it?” for the time is typically German; Greek asks τι ώρα είναι; (what hour is it?), like Wie viel Uhr ist es?
pitfalls: To be late = zu spät kommen (not *spät sein): Ich komme zu spät.
“Wie spät ist es?” asks the time – the answer is Es ist acht Uhr.
subtleties: später is its comparative and also the adverb “later”.
die Verspätung = the delay (of a train).

contrasts.value: only in immer noch / noch immer (stronger: still, even now)

profile.feeling: Every time, without exception – and “immer noch” when it still goes on.

senses.def: more and more (with a comparative: immer mehr)

examples.text: Ich trinke immer Tee am Morgen.
examples.tr: I always drink tea in the morning.
The bus is always full.
More and more tourists are coming.

examples.text: Er ist immer noch im Büro.
examples.tr: He’s still at the office.

etymology.text: From Middle High German iemer, from Old High German iomēr (“always”), from io (“ever”) + mēr (“more”). Cognate with Dutch immer.

funFacts: immer is literally “ever more” (io + mēr) – English “evermore” is built the same way.
pitfalls: immer noch / noch immer = still (not *immer alone): Er wartet immer noch.
Frequency words stand after the verb (and after a pronoun object): Ich trinke immer Tee.
subtleties: immer wieder = again and again; immer mit der Ruhe = take it easy.

profile.feeling: Again and again – a habit, a favourite place.

examples.tr: We often eat fish.
How often does the bus run?

examples.text: Ich bin nicht oft zu Hause.
examples.tr: I’m not often at home.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ofte, oft, from Old High German ofta, ofto, from Proto-Germanic *ufta. Cognate with Dutch oft, English oft and often.

funFacts: oft is English oft (as in oft-quoted) – English added -en to make often.
pitfalls: Comparative öfter (more often), with umlaut: Ich komme öfter.
Wie oft? asks how often: Wie oft trinkst du Kaffee? – Dreimal am Tag.
subtleties: öfter alone also means “now and then, quite often”: Ich sehe ihn öfter.

profile.feeling: Now and then – not always, not never.

examples.text: Manchmal fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad.
examples.tr: Sometimes I go by bike.
We sometimes eat at a restaurant.

examples.text: Manchmal ist es besser, zu warten.
examples.tr: Sometimes it’s better to wait.

etymology.text: From manch (“some, many a”) + Mal (“time, occasion”).

funFacts: manchmal is literally “some times” – exactly the English sometimes, piece by piece.
pitfalls: manchmal is one word, lower case.
At the start it pushes the verb before the subject: Manchmal fahre ich … (not *Manchmal ich fahre …).
subtleties: das Mal (time, occasion) builds einmal (once), zweimal (twice), jedes Mal (every time), manchmal (some times).

contrasts.value: the adverb: every morning, or a.m. (um sieben Uhr morgens)

lexemes.role: in the mornings, every morning (habit) – adverb from der Morgen; compare morgen = tomorrow

profile.feeling: Every morning, as a habit – coffee at seven, the bus at eight.

senses.def: a.m. (with a time: um sieben Uhr morgens)

examples.tr: In the mornings I drink coffee.

examples.text: Ich gehe morgens zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: I walk to work in the mornings.

examples.text: Der Zug fährt um sechs Uhr morgens.
examples.tr: The train leaves at six in the morning.

synonyms.nuance: in the morning – one morning or in general

etymology.text: From Middle High German morgens, adverbial genitive of morgen (modern der Morgen). Equivalent to Morgen + -s.

funFacts: The -s is an old genitive (“of the morning”), like English “of a morning” or the -s of English nowadays.
pitfalls: morgens (lower case, -s) = in the mornings, as a habit; am Morgen = in the morning (one or in general); morgen = tomorrow.
subtleties: The same pattern: mittags, nachmittags, abends, nachts, montags, sonntags – all habitual, all lower case.

contrasts.value: the adverb: every evening, or p.m.

lexemes.role: in the evenings, every evening (habit) – adverb from der Abend

profile.feeling: Every evening – dinner, the news, a walk.

senses.def: p.m. (with a time: um acht Uhr abends)

examples.tr: In the evenings we eat together.
I’m often tired in the evenings.

examples.text: Das Restaurant ist bis zehn Uhr abends offen.
examples.tr: The restaurant is open until ten in the evening.

synonyms.nuance: in the evening – one evening or in general

etymology.text: From Middle High German ābendes, adverbial genitive of ābent (modern der Abend). From Abend + -s.

funFacts: Like morgens, abends is an old genitive: “of an evening”.
pitfalls: abends (lower case) = in the evenings, as a habit; am Abend = in the evening; heute Abend = this evening.
subtleties: German has no a.m./p.m.: it says morgens / abends or uses the 24-hour clock: um 20 Uhr.
